intro.t: Rescue from slavery, the law at Sinai, and God moving in.
b: The central act of the Old Testament. God hears, remembers his covenant, and brings Israel out of Egypt by power. Then at Sinai he gives them a law — not as a means of earning rescue, which has already happened, but as the shape of life for a people already redeemed. The order matters and is easy to get backwards.
The last third, often skipped, concerns the tabernacle in exhausting detail. The payoff is the final verse: God comes to live in the middle of the camp. That is the point of the whole book.

3.t: The bush burns without being consumed. God identifies himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob — by relationship before by attribute.
The name given is deliberately open: I am who I am. Jesus' 'before Abraham was, I am' reaches back here.

6.t: God's answer to Moses' complaint is a chain of first-person promises. Redemption is entirely his initiative.

12.t: The lamb without defect, the blood on the doorposts, the judgement passing over. Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb; John notes that no bone of his was broken.
Without defect, blood on the doorframes, the meal eaten ready to travel. Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb.

14.t: Stand firm and see the salvation of the LORD. Israel contributes nothing to the rescue except walking through it.

19.t: The identity given to Israel at Sinai, and the words Peter applies to the church.
The people are warned not to touch the mountain. Hebrews 12 contrasts this scene with the one believers have come to.

20.t: Note the preface: I am the LORD your God who brought you out of Egypt. The law follows the rescue rather than earning it.
The people ask Moses to speak instead. Fear of God is right; this is what it looks like when it goes wrong.

32.t: Six weeks after Sinai. Aaron's account of how it happened is one of the feeblest excuses in Scripture.
Moses offers himself in their place. Paul says something similar about Israel in Romans 9.

33.h: I will not go with you
33.t: God offers the land without his presence. Moses refuses the offer, which is the right answer and not an obvious one.
God passes by and proclaims his own name. Mark uses this 'passing by' language of Jesus on the water.

40.t: The book ends with God moving in. Everything Exodus has been building toward is this.

4.t: Moses objects repeatedly and God answers each one, until the LORD's anger burns and Aaron is appointed. Reluctance is met patiently and then firmly.

7.t: The stated purpose throughout is that Egypt will know that he is the LORD. Each plague is aimed at a god the Egyptians worshipped.

15.t: Israel's oldest poem. Miriam leads the women with tambourines. Revelation 15 calls the final song the song of Moses.

16.t: Enough for the day, and it rots if hoarded. Jesus draws on this in John 6, and the Lord's Prayer asks for daily bread.

17.t: Paul says the rock was Christ. Note that God stands on the rock and tells Moses to strike it — the blow falls where God is.
Aaron and Hur support Moses' arms until sunset. A picture of what holding one another up actually looks like.

24.t: Half the blood on the altar, half on the people. Jesus takes this exact phrase at the Last Supper. Then the elders see God and eat.

34.t: Compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness — and by no means clearing the guilty. The most quoted self-description of God in the Old Testament.

1.h: A king who did not know Joseph
1.t: The midwives Shiphrah and Puah defy him and are named in Scripture, while the Pharaoh is not.

2.h: Forty years on the back of a desert
2.t: Moses' attempt to deliver Israel by his own hand fails completely. God hears, remembers, sees and knows — four verbs that set up everything after.

5.t: The first result of obedience is heavier work and the people turning on Moses. He takes the complaint straight to God.

13.t: God deliberately avoids the short road so they will not face war and turn back. Guidance is not always the direct route.

8.t: From the third plague the magicians cannot copy it and admit it is the finger of God. Pharaoh's hardening is described both as his own doing and as God's — Scripture holds both without resolving them. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

9.t: A distinction is now made between Egypt and Israel. Some of Pharaoh's officials fear the word of the LORD and bring their animals in — faith appearing even in Egypt.

Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart and that God hardened it, and the sequence matters. God announces in advance, before any plague, that he will harden Pharaoh's heart (4:21, 7:3); through the first five plagues the text describes Pharaoh hardening his own; from 9:12 it says the LORD hardened it. The historic Reformed reading is that God's announced purpose and Pharaoh's real choices are both true, and that God gave him over to a resistance he had already chosen — confirming a hard heart rather than corrupting a willing one. Others hold that God's hardening is judicial withdrawal, letting Pharaoh have his way. Paul takes up the episode in Romans 9 to show God's freedom in mercy, and answers the objection it raises rather than removing it. Scripture holds sovereignty and responsibility together without resolving the tension, and so should we. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

10.t: Pharaoh's negotiations narrow each time: go, but not far; go, but leave the children; go, but leave the flocks. The demand from God never shrinks.

11.t: The death of the firstborn, the gravest thing in the book and the hardest to read. It answers Pharaoh's own slaughter of Hebrew boys in chapter 1, and Israel's firstborn are spared only by the blood. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

18.t: Moses is judging the people from morning to evening, and his father-in-law tells him plainly it will wear him out. The origin of delegated leadership, taken from a Midianite priest.

21.t: Case law for an ancient society, including rules on slavery that regulate an existing institution rather than approve it. 'Eye for eye' was a limit on revenge, not a licence for it. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

21.h: Does the Bible approve of slavery
21.t: The honest answer is that the law regulated an institution that existed everywhere in the ancient world rather than abolishing it, as Jesus said of divorce, because of hardness of heart. The hardest texts must be faced first. Leviticus 25:44–46 permits buying foreign slaves as inheritable property for life, on different terms from Hebrew servants who went free after six years. Exodus 21:20–21 penalises a master who kills a slave outright but not one whose slave survives a day or two, adding the chilling reason that the slave is his property. Christians should not explain these away. Alongside them stand provisions unlike anything in surrounding law codes: kidnapping a person to sell was a capital crime (21:16), an injured slave went free (21:26–27), and a runaway was not to be returned (Deuteronomy 23:15). The New Testament never commands slavery and plants principles that undid it — every person made in God's image, no slave or free in Christ, Philemon receiving Onesimus as a brother — which Wilberforce and the abolitionists drew on directly. Christians have answered the remaining difficulty in different ways: that God accommodated law to a hard society while pointing beyond it, or that these regulations limited an evil he did not yet abolish. Neither answer makes the texts comfortable. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

22.h: The widow, the orphan and the foreigner
22.t: God says he will hear their cry himself. The concern for the vulnerable is built into the law code from its first pages.

23.t: Do not follow the crowd in doing wrong, do not favour the poor or the rich in a lawsuit, do not take a bribe. Remarkably modern in its demands.

25.t: Seven chapters of design. The point is stated in verse 8: make a sanctuary so I may dwell among them. Hebrews reads the whole structure as a copy of the heavenly reality.

26.t: The curtain separating the Most Holy Place is the one torn from top to bottom at the crucifixion.

27.t: Placed first as you entered — nobody approaches God without passing sacrifice.

28.t: He carries the names of the twelve tribes on his shoulders and over his heart. Hebrews presents Jesus as the priest who carries his people in the same way.

29.t: Seven days of consecration, ending with the promise that God will dwell among them and be their God — the covenant formula repeated through the whole Bible.

30.t: The atonement money is the same for rich and poor: every life costs the same to redeem.

31.t: The first person in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God, and it is for craftsmanship. Skilled work is presented as a spiritual gift.

35.t: The materials come as freewill offerings, from men and women alike. Chapter 36 records that they had to be told to stop giving.

36.t: The only recorded occasion in Scripture where people were restrained from giving.

37.h: The ark and the mercy seat
37.t: The lid of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. Paul uses the same word for Christ in Romans 3:25.

38.t: An exact reckoning of the metals used. Public accountability for money given to God, recorded in Scripture.

39.t: Said repeatedly. Moses inspects the work and blesses the people — obedience and blessing together.
